criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. The study examines intergovernmental policy implementation of municipal wastewater treatment plant construction and operation for point-source water pollution control under the U.S. Clean Water Act.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes) because it examines institutional, regulatory, and governance arrangements—specifically complete privatization via municipal service contracts versus federal EPA construction grant funding and NPDES permitting in municipal wastewater treatment. However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow=no) because those ownership, contracting, and grant rules are examined solely as mechanisms governing treatment plant construction, effluent pollution control, workforce/labor practices, and municipal contract autonomy, not as rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community service access. Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical evidence from a comparative matched-case study of 13 U.S. locales (5 privatized cities, 5 matched grant-funded cities, and 3 additional privatized cases) using an 18-page semi-structured on-site interview questionnaire, legal/contractual documents, and two EPA databases (PCS and GICS).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports no outcome relevant to household or community service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. Reported outcomes are limited to treatment plant construction time, effluent water-quality compliance (pollutant removal), local operator workforce capacity, innovative plant technology, plant workforce AA/EEO demographics, labor/union wages and bargaining, and municipal autonomy/accountability.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (13 U.S. municipal wastewater treatment implementation structures), exposure (complete privatization vs. federal EPA construction grants), non-access implementation outcomes, and study design (matched-case comparative implementation study) are all clearly identifiable for the study's own research question, though no household/community service-access outcome is measured.

study_design: Comparative matched-case implementation study (semi-structured interviews, documentary analysis, and EPA administrative databases)
population_and_sample: 13 U.S. municipalities implementing wastewater treatment facilities (5 privatized cities matched with 5 EPA grant-funded cities across four U.S. states, plus 3 additional privatized cities in three states; unit of analysis: intergovernmental implementation structure / municipal treatment plant)
exposure: Complete privatization (private design, construction, ownership, operation, and maintenance) versus federal EPA Clean Water Act construction grant funding of municipal wastewater treatment plants
outcome: Plant construction duration, NPDES effluent water-quality compliance, local operator workforce capacity, innovative plant technology adoption, plant employee AA/EEO demographics (minority and female workforce percentages), labor/union impacts, and local governmental autonomy and accountability (no household or community service-access outcome)
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails c1 and narrow c2). Although this empirical matched-case study examines municipal wastewater treatment privatization versus federal EPA construction grants in 13 U.S. cities, it investigates point-source environmental pollution control and organizational goal multiplicity rather than household or community sanitation service access. All reported outcomes—plant construction speed, NPDES effluent compliance, operator training, plant technology innovation, employee AA/EEO demographics, union/wage impacts, and municipal contract autonomy—are plant-level environmental, labor, or intergovernmental implementation outcomes, with no outcome measuring household or community access, sewer connection, service availability, reliability, affordability, or exclusion. Under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording, the study is excluded.
